data.text/html:
Rapid deduplication & fuzzy matching with the Fellegi-Sunter model

An interactive companion to Robin Linacre's PyData talk on Splink. Three messy records all say Lucas Smith, but there's no person ID that ties them together. Below you'll build, from scratch in numpy and pandas, the same pipeline Splink uses: fuzzy matching → term frequencies → m/u probabilities → blocking → Fellegi-Sunter scoring (waterfall) → clustering.Colour language used throughout ■ teal = evidence for a match (positive match weight) · ■ coral = evidence against a match (negative weight) · ■ purple = the prior / final score · ■ orange = the thing you're currently looking at

data.text/markdown:
1 · The problem: no unique ID

Records about the same entity get collected without a unique identifier: within one dataset (deduplication) or across several (linkage). Robin's point is that both are the same problem: stack the tables and dedupe. The plan, at a very high level:
  1. Pairwise comparisons: compare record i with record j and predict a match probability.
  2. These predictions form a graph: records are nodes, probable matches are edges.
  3. Connected components of that graph are clusters, and each one gets a new person_id.
Below is a synthetic dataset built for this notebook, in the spirit of Splink's "historical people" demo: about 1,200 true people, each with 1–5 records corrupted by typos, nicknames, missing values, a 7↔1 date slip, and a data-quality landmine (Sir Baronet). The hidden true_id column is the ground truth; the model never sees it.

data.text/markdown:
2 · Information source #1: fuzzy matching

Functions like Levenshtein and Jaro-Winkler look at one column of one pair and return a distance or a similarity.
  • Levenshtein: how many single-character edits turn a into b? smith → smyth is 1. It's a dynamic program: ||(D[i,j] = \min\big(D[i-1,j]+1,\; D[i,j-1]+1,\; D[i-1,j-1] + [a_i \ne b_j]\big)||)
  • Jaro-Winkler: a similarity on a 0–1 scale that counts matching characters within a window, penalises transpositions, and gives a bonus for a shared prefix (names are rarely mistyped at the start).
Step through the Levenshtein table. Each cell is the cheapest way to turn a prefix of a into a prefix of b. The orange cell is being filled, and its three neighbours (delete ↓, insert →, substitute ↘) are outlined.

They only look at the two values \u003cem\u003ein isolation\u003c/em\u003e. Section 3 fixes that.\u003c/li\u003e\n\u003c/ul\u003e\u003c/span\u003e"' data-kind='"info"'></marimo-callout-output>

data.text/markdown:
3 · Information source #2: term frequencies (coincidences)

A match on Smith is weaker evidence than a match on Linacre, because two different people share the surname Smith by coincidence far more often. Fellegi-Sunter (section 6) scores agreement with a Bayes factor ||(m/u||):
  • ||(m||) = P(agree | records are a match)
  • ||(u||) = P(agree | records are a non-match), i.e. the chance of a coincidence
For an exact match on a specific value ||(v||), the coincidence rate is roughly the value's term frequency ||(f_v||), so the term-frequency-adjusted match weight is ||[w_v = \log_2 \frac{m}{f_v} \qquad\text{vs. the average}\qquad \bar w = \log_2\frac{m}{\sum_v f_v^2}||]Pick a column and a value. The orange bar is your value, and the right-hand chart shows how much an exact match on it is worth.

data.text/markdown:
4 · Information source #3: data quality, the m probabilities

How often do values differ among true matches? Robin's example is two dates of birth for Lucas that differ by one character, a 7 vs a 1 (July vs January).
  • If the data was typed from handwritten records, that slip happens all the time. A 1-character difference is then positive evidence for a match.
  • If the dates came from driving licences, they're almost never wrong. The same difference is then strong evidence against.
Each comparison level ||(\ell||) gets its own weight ||(w_\ell = \log_2 \dfrac{m_\ell}{u_\ell}||). A full disagreement gets ||(\log_2 \dfrac{1-m}{1-u}||), which is negative, and that's information that is often thrown away. First, the general relationship: drag ||(m||) and ||(u||).

data.text/html: Agreeing multiplies the odds by 95.0×; disagreeing multiplies them by 0.0505×.

data.text/markdown:
5 · Blocking: beating the ||(n^2||) problem

Comparing every record with every other gives ||(n(n-1)/2||) pairs: 2.5 billion for Robin's 50,000 rows. Blocking keeps only pairs that share some cheap key, e.g. l.first_name = r.first_name. Blocking is about recall, not precision. It should quickly throw away the obvious non-matches; the scoring model decides the rest. We use a list of rules (pairs found by any rule are kept), because a single rule like "first names equal" would silently drop every nickname and typo before it was ever scored. Tick rules on and off, and toggle the data cleaning. Splink-style, each bar counts only the new comparisons a rule adds.

data.text/html: Which key values generate the most comparisons for rule first_name & surname?

Flip \u003cstrong\u003eclean titles\u003c/strong\u003e on and watch it disappear.\u003c/li\u003e\n\u003cli\u003eAdd the \u003ccode\u003eoccupation\u003c/code\u003e rule and you hit the safety brake. Splink checks counts \u003cem\u003ebefore\u003c/em\u003e materialising pairs, and so does this cell (it uses \u003cmarimo-tex class=\"arithmatex\"\u003e||(\\sum_k \\binom{k}{2}||)\u003c/marimo-tex\u003e per key).\u003c/li\u003e\n\u003cli\u003eUse only \u003ccode\u003efirst_name &amp; surname\u003c/code\u003e. Precision rises but \u003cstrong\u003erecall\u003c/strong\u003e drops, because every typo'd name is gone before scoring.\u003c/li\u003e\n\u003c/ul\u003e\u003c/span\u003e"' data-kind='"info"'></marimo-callout-output>

data.text/markdown:
6 · Fellegi-Sunter: adding up match weights, learned without labels

We now have the three ingredients: similarity levels per column (source 1), u from coincidences (source 2), and m from data quality (source 3). Fellegi-Sunter combines them, assuming the columns are conditionally independent: ||[\underbrace{\log_2\frac{\lambda}{1-\lambda}}_{\text{prior}} \;+\; \sum_{\text{columns } c} \underbrace{\log_2\frac{m_{c,\ell}}{u_{c,\ell}}}_{\text{match weight}} \;=\; \text{match score}\quad\Rightarrow\quad P(\text{match}) = \frac{2^{\text{score}}}{1+2^{\text{score}}}||]No labels are needed. Like Splink, we estimate u from random pairs (done in section 4) and then m with Expectation-Maximisation on blocked pairs. As in Splink, we run one EM session per blocking rule and learn only the columns that the rule did not force to agree (block on name → learn DOB/city/occupation; block on DOB → learn the names):
  • E-step: score every pair with the current ||(m||) and get ||(p_k = P(\text{match}\mid\gamma_k)||).
  • M-step: ||(m_{c,\ell} = \dfrac{\sum_k p_k\,[\gamma_{k,c}=\ell]}{\sum_k p_k}||), and ||(\lambda = \text{mean}(p_k)||).
Scrub through the EM iterations. Bars are the learned weights; the black ticks are the true weights computed from the hidden labels, which EM never sees.

data.text/markdown:
7 · Reading one prediction: the waterfall chart

Robin's favourite way to explain a prediction: reach into a box of all records, pull out two in sealed envelopes. Before you look, the chance they match is the prior (about 1 in 1,500 here, so a very negative weight). Then you open the envelopes one column at a time, and each comparison adds its match weight. The running total is the match score; above 0 bits the pair is more likely a match than not. Load a real pair, then click the level chips to ask "what if DOB had matched exactly?" (this is the match-weights chart and the waterfall in one).

data.text/markdown:
8 · From pairwise predictions to a new person ID: clustering

Pairwise predictions form a graph: records are nodes, and pairs above a probability threshold are edges. Each connected component becomes an estimated cluster, which is the person_id the data never had. This is transitive: if A–B and B–C are linked, A and C end up in the same cluster even if they were never compared directly. Slide the threshold and watch the precision/recall trade-off (labels are hidden from the model and used here only to score it). Below that, one neighbourhood is drawn as a graph.

data.text/markdown:
Recap

Step Idea Formula / rule Where you touched it
Fuzzy matching similarity of two values in isolation Levenshtein DP, Jaro-Winkler §2 DP stepper
Term frequency coincidences depend on the value ||(w_v = \log_2(m / f_v)||) §3 Smith vs Linacre
Data quality how often true matches disagree ||(m_\ell||), and ||(\log_2\frac{1-m}{1-u}||) for disagreement §4 handwritten vs licence
Blocking avoid ||(n^2||), keep recall union of l.x = r.x rules, ||(\sum_k \binom{k}{2}||) pre-count §5 rule picker
Fellegi-Sunter add up independent evidence ||(\text{score} = \log_2\frac{\lambda}{1-\lambda} + \sum_c \log_2\frac{m_{c,\ell}}{u_{c,\ell}}||) §6 EM scrubber
Unsupervised training no labels needed u by random sampling, m by EM per blocking rule §6
Explainability one prediction = a sum of bars waterfall / match-weights chart §7 clickable waterfall
Clustering pairs → entities connected components above a threshold §8 graph + P/R curve
What this notebook simplifies vs. real Splink: SQL backends (DuckDB/Spark) for scale, many more comparison templates, TF adjustments on fuzzy levels, and per-rule λ estimation. The maths is the same.
